title: Every square wears a points forecast
allegory: A value function is like a sticky note on every square of a board game saying how many points you will collect from there on, on average, if you keep playing your usual way, with points later counting a little less.
map: your usual way of choosing moves
the note: points still to come from here, on average
V_π(s) = E[Σ γᵗ rₜ | s₀ = s]
a point next turn is worth 0.9 of a point now
each note = this turn's points + 0.9 × the next squares' notes, averaged
the Bellman equation V(s) = E[r + γV(s′)]
credit: The one-dimensional corridor of states with discounted returns echoes Andrew Ng's Mars rover example in the Machine Learning Specialization's reinforcement learning week.

props.label: how good is it to stand here?

cap.1: Standing on one square of a game board, how good is it to be here? It depends on the points still to come, and on how you tend to play.
cap.2: A value function scores each state by the reward you can expect from there onwards, following a given policy. It's how an RL agent judges situations, not just moves.
cap.3: V_π(s) = E_π[Σ γᵗ rₜ | s₀ = s]: the expected discounted return from s under π. It depends on both the environment's dynamics and the policy.

cap.1: Put a sticky note on every square: the points you'll collect from here on, on average, playing your usual way. Points later count a bit less.
cap.2: V(s) is that note. The policy is your usual way of playing; the average is over dice rolls and your own random choices; the discount γ makes later points count less.
cap.3: The expectation runs over the policy's action distribution and the environment's transitions; γ in [0, 1) keeps the infinite sum finite and encodes a preference for sooner reward.

cap.1: Each note equals this turn's points plus a discounted average of the notes where you might land next. Every note is pinned down by its neighbours' notes.
cap.2: That self-consistency is the Bellman equation. Sweep it as an update from all zeros and the notes settle; with γ < 1 they always converge to the true values.
cap.3: The Bellman operator is a γ-contraction in the sup norm, so sweeps converge to the unique fixed point V_π. With π fixed it's linear: v = (I − γP)⁻¹r in one solve (Howard, 1960).

cap.1: A corridor with treasure at the end. Sweep the notes again and again: the good news spreads backwards one square per sweep, shrinking by 0.9 each step.
cap.2: Synchronous Bellman sweeps from zeros. Walking right earns +1 on reaching the treasure, so values settle at 1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.73: the discount compounding once per step.
cap.3: Each sweep applies the Bellman operator once, so information travels one transition per sweep. Fixed point: V = γ^(k−1) at k steps from the goal, matching the exact linear solve.

chapters.name: Square or exit?

left.title: V(s)
lines: to act on it you need the map

right.title: Q(s, a)
lines: how good is leaving this way

chapters.verdict: V judges situations; Q judges moves, which is what lets you act greedily.

cap.1: A note on the square says how good it is to stand here. A note on each exit says how good it is to leave that way. Only exit notes tell you which way to go.
cap.2: V is the value of a state under the policy; Q is the value of a state-action pair. Choosing greedily needs Q, or V plus a model of where each action leads.
cap.3: Policy improvement sets π'(s) = argmax_a Σ T(s′|s,a)(R + γV(s′)), which is greedy in Q_π. Model-free methods learn Q directly because they have no T for that lookahead.

cap.1: If later points count fully, notes around a loop can grow forever and never settle. A little discount is what keeps the forecast finite.
cap.2: With γ = 1 the Bellman update stops being a contraction: no guaranteed fixed point, and (I − γP) is singular. Keep γ < 1 in the tabular exercises.
cap.3: γ < 1 bounds returns by r_max/(1 − γ) and makes the operator a contraction. Also break argmax ties deterministically, or policy iteration can flip between equally good policies forever.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The critic in actor-critic is a learned V
RLHF gives a language model a value head

cap.1: Nearly every modern RL method keeps a forecaster like this beside the decision-maker, including the methods used to fine-tune chatbots.
cap.2: Actor-critic methods learn V as the critic, PPO uses it to judge whether an action beat expectations, and RLHF adds a value head to a language model for the same job.
cap.3: Advantages (Q − V, estimated from V via GAE) are how policy gradients assign credit. Understanding and steering RL-trained models means knowing what their value estimates reward.

coda.title: How far does the treasure's pull reach?

curves.label: V at x steps from the treasure

caption.1: Drag the discount and watch how fast the treasure's pull fades with distance. Add a cost per step and far squares can be worth less than nothing.
caption.2: V shrinks by a factor γ per step from the goal: γ near 1 means patient, far-sighted values; small γ means only nearby reward registers. Step costs pile up with distance.
caption.3: Closed form here: V(d) = γ^(d−1) − c(1 − γ^d)/(1 − γ). The effective horizon 1/(1 − γ) sets how far credit propagates, so γ decides what an agent learns to care about.

hamming.what: A number for every state: the expected discounted reward from there onwards if you keep following a given policy.
hamming.when: Whenever an agent must judge situations rather than single moves: planning, actor-critic, PPO and RLHF all keep one.
hamming.why: It compresses a long, uncertain future into one number per state, which lets credit flow backwards and lets you compare plans.

object.title: The forecast board
object.subtitle: A 6×6 board with treasure in one corner; each tower is that square's value under 'walk straight to the treasure'.

cap.1: A 6×6 board with treasure in the corner. Each tower's height is that square's forecast if you walk straight to the treasure.
cap.2: V_π for a deterministic shortest-path policy with +1 on arrival, γ = 0.9.
cap.3: V(s) = γ^(k−1) where k is the Manhattan distance to the goal.

cap.1: From above, the forecast forms diamond rings: every square the same number of steps away gets the same value.
cap.2: Level sets of V are the squares at equal step-distance from the goal.
cap.3: Under a shortest-path policy, V depends on s only through k(s), so contours follow the Manhattan metric.

cap.1: Make later points worth much less and the forecast drops to almost nothing a few steps out. A short-sighted agent.
cap.2: γ = 0.5: value halves with every step of distance.
cap.3: Small γ gives an effective horizon of about 2 steps; distant reward barely registers in V.

cap.1: Make later points worth nearly as much as now and the whole board glows. A patient agent.
cap.2: γ = 0.99: even the far corner keeps most of the treasure's value.
cap.3: As γ → 1 the effective horizon 1/(1 − γ) grows to 100 steps and V flattens.

cap.1: From the side, each step away multiplies the height by γ. That's the Bellman equation built in towers.
cap.2: Each tower is γ times its neighbour one step nearer the treasure.
cap.3: V(s) = r + γV(s′) with r = 0 off the goal: consecutive towers along the path differ by a factor γ.

predict.q: γ = 0.9. The treasure is 3 steps away and pays +1 on arrival, nothing else. What is V?
predict.why: The reward arrives on the third step, discounted twice: γ² = 0.81.

predict.q: What can change V(s) without changing the board at all?

options.t: Nothing: V is a property of the board

predict.why: V_π is the value under a given policy. Play differently and the forecast changes.

predict.q: Why keep γ < 1 in the tabular exercises?

options.t: It makes the Bellman update a contraction, so values converge

predict.why: With γ = 1, returns can be unbounded and (I − γP) is singular.

object.where: Any discounted forecast: present value in finance, critics in actor-critic, value heads in RLHF.
